reverse_outline.summary: Chapter promise: what 'in stock' means, who computes it, and why Kestrel & Pine oversold 1,340 jackets.
Key points: in stock is a derived promise, oversells come from multiple writers and lag, and one availability service publishes per-channel figures.
Failure patterns addressed: Phantom Stock, First Snowfall and Secret Agent.
Two channels selling the last jacket at once need a shared way to decide which sale gets it.
A shelf count is not enough; availability must combine commitments, holds and reservations before a sale.
Places availability in Eva's journey: the stock label, cart check and checkout commitment.
Roadmap of the chapter from the Black Friday Oversell to options, remedy, failures and count accuracy.

reverse_outline.summary: Walmart's event backend shows the same design at scale: one ordered stream per item and store.
Introduces four ways to compute availability, each fitting a stage.
Option 1: the platform's own stock, fine with one location and one order taker.
Option 2: ERP or WMS master with periodic sync, common but structurally laggy.
Option 3: an event-driven availability service, bought or built, costing integration work and discipline.
Option 4: a fulfillment provider's shared pool, such as ZEOS, trading control for simplicity.
Table comparing the four options on lag, writers, buffers, cost and failure mode.
Keep platform stock until another system counts or takes orders, then agree owners before building connectors.
Adopt an availability service when two complexity conditions hold (as Kestrel & Pine did in 2023), and a provider pool suits provider-dominant sellers.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Across scale stages the invariants stay; Omnichannel merchants must arrange them deliberately.
The reconstruction reveals three causes of the Oversell, each answered by W1.
Cause 1, lag by design, replaced by stock events through the iPaaS.
Cause 2, six writers, replaced by one named writer per state and apps losing inventory rights.
Cause 3, no buffer and no reconciliation, fixed with per-channel buffers and weekly reconciliation that found 2.3% drift.
Replaying the evening with W1 shrinks the oversell to a handful; the goal is a narrow window and deliberate buffer.
Table of recurring stock-integration failures with detection and recovery.
Every stock integration needs a reconciliation job because delivery is never guaranteed (W5).
Reconciliation cannot fix wrong counts, and research shows inventory records are often inaccurate.
Cycle counting and safety buffers control count accuracy.
Callback to the opening: one owner per fact, one derivation, atomic checkout commit, decided in writing.
Established findings: separated stock numbers, configurable promise timing, inaccurate counts and at-least-once delivery.
Context-dependent guidance on platform stock, periodic sync, reserve-on-cart and buy versus build.
Author's synthesis: decide stock ownership in writing first and size buffers from measured error and lag.
Eight questions to probe ownership, writers, promise timing, propagation, buffers, reconciliation and outages.
Part II's five incidents are one problem: systems using values they did not own, unchecked.
The shared remedy (one writer, declared path, reconciliation) and an exercise to list owners per fact, starting with stock.
Hand-off to Part III: Eva's committed jacket moves into cart, checkout and payment.
